floor_history.headline: Recon: floor 24 is 100% register+ordering (141/141 insns) in exactly two clusters; 3 hypotheses killed, and the cluster-1 allocation flip is PROVEN reachable (a live-range extension of `i` put `src` i

Cluster 1's i/src register inversion is CLOSED as an allocation problem: exact global.c priority model measured, requirement L_i > 1.222*L_src proven unreachable (max 1.088), find_reg steering shown i

Cluster 2 is invariant under source statement order — all 24 permutations of its four independent statements measured; the residual is a sched1 INSN_PRIORITY effect, and `s8 val` read last is now posi

frontier.hypothesis: Cluster 2's residual is entirely sched1's decision to hoist insn 134 (the p[8] load) above insn 128 (the D_80102784 store); target's compile had that hoist blocked or outranked, and the block's INSN_PRIORITY values will say which.
frontier.mechanism: sched1 interleaving the two extraction chains gives them overlapping live ranges, so lreg must give the second chain $v1 instead of reusing $v0, and sched2 then emits the interleaved order. A non-interleaved sched1 output is exactly what target's strictly-$v0-serialized block requires. Since all 24 source orders give the identical schedule, the decision is made on INSN_PRIORITY (or on a memory dependence that our compile does not have), not on program order.
frontier.next_probe: Add a function-name filter to the BB2_RANK_DEBUG hook path (or bracket the dump per function) so tmp/grind/func_8003504C/s3/rank.sh reports only func_8003504C, and read the actual INSN_PRIORITY and readiness of insns 128/131/134/146 in that block. Then attack whichever knob the numbers implicate — a source spelling that lengthens the p[5] chain or shortens the p[8] chain, or one that creates a real memory dependence between the D_80102784 store and the p[8] load. Do NOT re-run any statement-order variant; all 24 are measured.

frontier.hypothesis: Target's pre-loop block cannot be produced by scheduling our RTL at all — its RTL differs structurally, because `move $t3,$v0` (lowest LUID, feeds `move $a2,$t3`, hence strictly higher priority than a bare constant) is emitted AFTER `li 5` / `li 20` in target and before them in ours.
frontier.mechanism: sched1 picks the highest-priority ready insn; a copy that feeds another copy outranks a zero-dependent constant load, so under our RTL the constants can never precede it. Either the constants have in-block dependents in target's RTL (a use we do not have), or the pre-loop region is split differently into basic blocks, or the copies are created later in the chain (e.g. by loop.c) than ours are.
frontier.next_probe: Read the pre-loop block boundaries and the per-insn priorities out of the .sched dump for the HEAD form (rtlblock.py already gives the compact listing; the boundaries come from the .flow dump's basic-block table), and specifically check what could give `li 5` / `li 20` an in-block dependent. vP3 already proved loop.c hoist order controls constants-vs-address ordering, so the remaining question is only about the two `move`s.

frontier.hypothesis: If the loop-1 counter is spelled so cc1 emits TWO pseudos for it (a split live range that reload coalesces back), cluster 1's allocation flip becomes reachable despite session 2's arithmetic closure.
frontier.mechanism: allocno priority is per-pseudo; a split induction variable halves both refs and live_length for each half, which can move one half below src's 27/L while the emitted addiu/slti stay identical if reload coalesces them back. This is the one premise session 2's model does not cover.
frontier.next_probe: Look for a natural C spelling in which the value consumed by the stores is a distinct pseudo from the one incremented, and read the .flow refs/live_length with tmp/grind/func_8003504C/s2/probe.sh BEFORE judging on score. Do not spend turns on any further init-order / loop-note / giv variant — all three are measured dead.
